pos: proper n. (one of the seventy elders who prophesied in the camp)
etymology: Hebrew 'eldad, from 'el, God, and dad, beloved: God hath loved or beloved of God.
biblical_def: Moses had complained that the burden of the people was too heavy, and God took of the spirit that was upon him and gave it to seventy elders gathered at the tabernacle. Two of the seventy did not come out. “But there remained two of the men in the camp, the name of the one was Eldad, and the name of the other Medad: and the spirit rested upon them; and they were of them that were written, but went not out unto the tabernacle: and they prophesied in the camp” (Numbers 11:26). Joshua was alarmed for his master's honour: “My lord Moses, forbid them” (Numbers 11:28). Moses answered with one of the most generous sayings in the Old Testament: “Enviest thou for my sake? would God that all the LORD'S people were prophets, and that the LORD would put his spirit upon them!” (Numbers 11:29). Eldad's prophesying was God's doing, and Moses would not guard his own office against God's gifts.

corruption_summary: Eldad and Medad are claimed as warrant for unordered, self-authenticating prophecy in the church today, when they were enrolled elders on whom God Himself put the Spirit.
corruption_paragraphs: Charismatic and New Apostolic writers cite Numbers 11 to argue that God pours out prophecy outside recognized order and that leaders who question it are Joshuas resisting the Spirit. The text says the two were of them that were written: they were among the seventy appointed elders, and the Spirit came on them by God's act, not their claim. Moses' wish was fulfilled at Pentecost, when the Spirit was poured on all flesh.

The dictionary is cessationist. With the canon complete, the church tests every claim by the written word and does not receive new revelation. The principle to recover from Moses is the absence of envy: a true servant rejoices when God honours others.

pos: proper n. (one of the seventy elders who prophesied in the camp)
etymology: Hebrew meydad, from yadad or dod, to love: love or beloved.
biblical_def: Medad is never named without Eldad, and the pair are remembered for one afternoon in the wilderness. When the news reached the tabernacle, “there ran a young man, and told Moses, and said, Eldad and Medad do prophesy in the camp” (Numbers 11:27). The young man, like Joshua after him, assumed that something irregular must be stopped. Moses saw instead the hand of God and longed for more of it: “would God that all the LORD'S people were prophets, and that the LORD would put his spirit upon them!” (Numbers 11:29). That longing became a promise through Joel: “I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy” (Joel 2:28), and Peter declared it fulfilled at Pentecost. Medad stands at the beginning of that line, a sign in the camp that the Spirit was not to remain on one man alone.

pos: proper n. (Midianite woman slain by Phinehas)
etymology: Hebrew kozbi, perhaps from kazab, to lie, to deceive: deceitful; though the name may be Midianite in origin.
biblical_def: Cozbi was the daughter of a Midianite prince, and her death ended a plague. Israel had joined itself to Baal-peor through the women of Moab and Midian, and while the congregation wept at the tabernacle door, “one of the children of Israel came and brought unto his brethren a Midianitish woman in the sight of Moses, and in the sight of all the congregation” (Numbers 25:6). Phinehas rose and thrust both of them through. The text names her with care: “And the name of the Midianitish woman that was slain was Cozbi, the daughter of Zur; he was head over a people, and of a chief house in Midian” (Numbers 25:15). Her rank showed that the seduction was policy, not accident, and God said so: “For they vex you with their wiles, wherewith they have beguiled you in the matter of Peor, and in the matter of Cozbi” (Numbers 25:18). Behind the wiles stood Balaam's counsel, who taught Balac to cast a stumblingblock before Israel.

corruption_summary: Phinehas' act is condemned as violent zealotry, when Scripture commends it as the zeal of God that turned away His wrath from Israel.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern moral sensibility recoils from Numbers 25 and treats Phinehas as a fanatic. Scripture's verdict is the opposite: God gave him the covenant of an everlasting priesthood because he was zealous for his God, and Psalm 106:31 says it was counted unto him for righteousness. The act was a judicial execution in a moment of open rebellion, during a plague that had already killed thousands.

The principle to recover is that seduction into idolatry is war against God's people, and that God hates the mixing of His worship with the worship of idols. Revelation 2:14 still warns the church against the doctrine of Balaam.

pos: proper n. (father of the prophet Micaiah)
etymology: Hebrew yimlah, from male', to fill: he will fill, or fulness.
biblical_def: Imlah is known only as the father of a prophet who would not lie. When Ahab and Jehoshaphat wanted counsel before Ramoth-gilead, four hundred prophets said Go up. Jehoshaphat wanted one more, and Ahab confessed the problem: “There is yet one man, Micaiah the son of Imlah, by whom we may enquire of the LORD: but I hate him; for he doth not prophesy good concerning me, but evil” (1 Kings 22:8). The messenger urged Micaiah to agree with the majority, and he answered: “As the LORD liveth, what the LORD saith unto me, that will I speak” (1 Kings 22:14). He foretold Ahab's death, was struck and imprisoned, and staked his ministry on the event: “If thou return at all in peace, the LORD hath not spoken by me” (1 Kings 22:28). Ahab died that day. The name of Imlah is preserved because his son preferred one word from God to the approval of four hundred.

pos: proper n. (father of Abdon the judge)
etymology: Hebrew hillel, from halal, to praise: he hath praised. The same root gives hallelujah.
biblical_def: The Hillel of Scripture is not the famous rabbi of the first century BC but a Pirathonite of the time of the judges, named only as a father. “And after him Abdon the son of Hillel, a Pirathonite, judged Israel” (Judges 12:13). Abdon judged eight years, and “Abdon the son of Hillel the Pirathonite died, and was buried in Pirathon in the land of Ephraim” (Judges 12:15). These quiet judges between the great deliverers are remembered by their fathers' names, their families and their graves. The book of Judges explains why such men existed at all: “Nevertheless the LORD raised up judges, which delivered them out of the hand of those that spoiled them” (Judges 2:16). Hillel's son was one of God's gifts in a dark age, and the father's name, he hath praised, is a fitting memorial.

pos: n. pl. (the star cluster in Taurus; Hebrew kimah)
etymology: Greek Pleiades, perhaps from plein, to sail, the cluster's rising marking the sailing season; the Hebrew is kimah, a cluster or heap.
biblical_def: The Pleiades appear in the Bible as proof that God made and governs the heavens. Job confesses the God “Which maketh Arcturus, Orion, and Pleiades, and the chambers of the south” (Job 9:9). Out of the whirlwind God asks Job the unanswerable question: “Canst thou bind the sweet influences of Pleiades, or loose the bands of Orion?” (Job 38:31). The cluster seemed bound together; Orion seemed bound in fetters; and no man could change either. Amos calls Israel to the same Creator: “Seek him that maketh the seven stars and Orion, and turneth the shadow of death into the morning” (Amos 5:8). The seven stars are the Pleiades, and the God who set them in their places is the God who turns death into morning. The stars do not rule men; their Maker rules the stars and men alike.

corruption_summary: The Pleiades were made objects of astrological power, as if they governed human fortunes, when Scripture names them only to glorify their Maker.
corruption_paragraphs: Ancient astrology assigned the Pleiades, like other stars, influence over seasons, births and destinies, and modern horoscope culture keeps the idea alive. Webster (1828) already called the doctrine of planetary influence exploded. Job 38:31 turns it upside down: the question is not what the stars can do to men but whether man can do anything to the stars.
The principle to recover is that the heavens declare the glory of God. The believer looks at the Pleiades and worships the Creator, and fears neither the stars nor the fates once ascribed to them.

pos: n. (Hebrew name of a constellation or the signs of the heavens)
etymology: Hebrew mazzarot, of uncertain meaning; most often taken as the constellations, or the signs of the zodiac, and related to mazzalot of 2 Kings 23:5, the planets.
biblical_def: Mazzaroth appears once, in God's interrogation of Job. “Canst thou bring forth Mazzaroth in his season? or canst thou guide Arcturus with his sons?” (Job 38:32). The question presses the same point as the one before it about the Pleiades and Orion: the movements of the heavens are in God's hand, and man cannot command a single star to rise. The next verse sharpens it: “Knowest thou the ordinances of heaven? canst thou set the dominion thereof in the earth?” (Job 38:33). There are ordinances of heaven, fixed laws of the created order, and God made them. The psalmist rejoices in the same truth: “He telleth the number of the stars; he calleth them all by their names” (Psalm 147:4). Whatever constellation Mazzaroth names, it marches on God's schedule, not man's.

corruption_paragraphs: Two errors meet at this word. Astrology claims that the signs govern human lives. A popular evangelical theory, the so-called gospel in the stars, claims that the zodiac preserves a primeval prophecy of Christ that can be read in the constellations. Both go beyond Scripture, which forbids divination by the heavens (Deuteronomy 18:10; Isaiah 47:13) and gives the gospel by the word, not by the stars.

The principle to recover is the sufficiency of Scripture and the sovereignty of the Creator. The heavens declare God's glory to all men, but they do not preach the name of Christ; that is the work of the written word.

pos: proper n. (an idol, a star-god worshipped by Israel)
etymology: Hebrew kiyyun, usually identified with the Akkadian Kaiwanu, the planet Saturn worshipped as a god. Stephen, following the Greek, calls it Remphan.
biblical_def: Amos indicts Israel with a secret history of idolatry reaching back to the wilderness. “Have ye offered unto me sacrifices and offerings in the wilderness forty years, O house of Israel?” (Amos 5:25). “But ye have borne the tabernacle of your Moloch and Chiun your images, the star of your god, which ye made to yourselves” (Amos 5:26). While God's tabernacle went before them, they carried shrines of star-gods behind them. Stephen quotes the charge in his defence before the council: “Yea, ye took up the tabernacle of Moloch, and the star of your god Remphan, figures which ye made to worship them: and I will carry you away beyond Babylon” (Acts 7:43). Chiun and Remphan name the same false god in two languages. The phrase which ye made to yourselves is the whole case against idolatry: a god a man makes is a god a man rules.

pos: proper n. (place in the valley of Megiddon; a byword for great mourning)
etymology: Hebrew hadad rimmon, joining the names of two Syrian storm-gods, Hadad and Rimmon; most likely the name of a town in the plain of Megiddo.
biblical_def: Zechariah compares the coming repentance of Jerusalem to the greatest mourning in Israel's memory. The LORD promises to pour the spirit of grace and supplications on the house of David, so that they look on Him whom they pierced and mourn. Then: “In that day shall there be a great mourning in Jerusalem, as the mourning of Hadadrimmon in the valley of Megiddon” (Zechariah 12:11). The reference is almost certainly to the death of Josiah, the last good king of Judah, struck down at Megiddo: “And all Judah and Jerusalem mourned for Josiah” (2 Chronicles 35:24). “And Jeremiah lamented for Josiah: and all the singing men and the singing women spake of Josiah in their lamentations to this day” (2 Chronicles 35:25). Zechariah takes that national grief over a fallen king and says it will be matched by Israel's grief over the pierced Shepherd, a mourning John sees fulfilled at the cross.

corruption_summary: Hadadrimmon is read as a pagan rite of mourning for a dying god, when the setting points to Israel's mourning for Josiah at Megiddo.
corruption_paragraphs: Because the name joins two divine names, some commentators make the mourning of Hadadrimmon a ritual lament for a fertility deity, like the weeping for Tammuz. Jerome identified it as a town near Megiddo, and the link with Josiah's death in the valley of Megiddo fits Zechariah's comparison of a national mourning for a king.

pos: proper n. (the twin gods on the figurehead of Paul’s ship)
etymology: Greek Dioskouroi, sons of Zeus, the twins Castor and Polydeuces (Latin Pollux) of Greek mythology, invoked by sailors as protectors at sea.
biblical_def: After the shipwreck Paul's party wintered on Melita, and then sailed on: “And after three months we departed in a ship of Alexandria, which had wintered in the isle, whose sign was Castor and Pollux” (Acts 28:11). The figurehead was a pair of pagan sea-gods, believed to rescue mariners in storms. Luke records it without comment, but the reader of chapter 27 knows who had actually saved every soul aboard the last ship: the God whose angel stood by Paul. The pagan world was quick to see gods everywhere, as at Lystra: “The gods are come down to us in the likeness of men” (Acts 14:11). Paul's answer to that world is in his letter to Corinth: “For though there be that are called gods, whether in heaven or in earth, (as there be gods many, and lords many,)” there is one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 8:5-6). The apostle sailed under the sign of the Twins, and served the one Lord who rules the sea.

corruption_paragraphs: The Twins survive as the constellation Gemini and in the astrological lore attached to it. Luke's detail is a mark of an eyewitness and a careful historian, consistent with the Alexandrian grain ships known to have wintered in Malta's harbours.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the uniqueness of the true God amid gods many. Christians live and travel in a world full of pagan signs, and fear none of them, because the Lord of the storm is their Saviour.
roots_summary: Greek Dioskouroi, Castor and Polydeuces, twin sons of Zeus, patrons of sailors; the sign of the ship at Acts 28:11.
roots_lines: Greek Dioskouroi, sons of Zeus.
Latin Pollux for Greek Polydeuces.
Acts 28:11 names the sign of the Alexandrian ship.
Acts 27:23-24 records the angel's promise to Paul in the storm.
1 Corinthians 8:5-6 contrasts gods many with one God and one Lord.
usage: whose sign was Castor and Pollux
the pagan sea-gods on Paul's ship
